::: {#exm-gibbs-bivariate-normal}
#### Gibbs sampling from a correlated Gaussian target

Let the target be the bivariate Gaussian distribution of $(\param_1, \param_2)$
with means 0, variances 1 and correlation $\corpar$,
whose density is proportional to
$\expf{-\frac{\param_1^2 - 2\corpar\param_1\param_2 + \param_2^2}{2(1-\corpar^2)}}$
[@CaseBerg01, Definition 4.5.10].
As a function of $\param_1$,

$$
\ba
\p(\param_1 \mid \param_2)
&\propto \expf{-\frac{\param_1^2 - 2\corpar\param_1\param_2}{2(1-\corpar^2)}}
&& \text{(dropping the factor with $\param_2^2$ only)}\\
&= \expf{-\frac{(\param_1 - \corpar\param_2)^2 - \corpar^2\param_2^2}{2(1-\corpar^2)}}
&& \text{(completing the square)}\\
&\propto \expf{-\frac{(\param_1 - \corpar\param_2)^2}{2(1-\corpar^2)}}
&& \text{(dropping the factor with $\param_2^2$ only)},
\ea
$$

so the [full conditional](#def-full-conditional) of $\param_1$
is $\ndist{\corpar\param_2,\, 1 - \corpar^2}$,
and by symmetry that of $\param_2$ is $\ndist{\corpar\param_1,\, 1 - \corpar^2}$.
We run the Gibbs sampler with $\corpar = 0$ and with $\corpar = 0.99$:

```{r}
#| label: gibbs-bivariate-normal
#| code-fold: false
gibbs_bvn <- function(n_iter, rho) {
  draws <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n_iter, ncol = 2)
  theta <- c(0, 0)
  cond_sd <- sqrt(1 - rho^2)
  for (t in seq_len(n_iter)) {
    theta[1] <- stats::rnorm(1, mean = rho * theta[2], sd = cond_sd)
    theta[2] <- stats::rnorm(1, mean = rho * theta[1], sd = cond_sd)
    draws[t, ] <- theta
  }
  draws
}

set.seed(3)
draws_indep <- gibbs_bvn(n_iter = 2000, rho = 0)
draws_corr <- gibbs_bvn(n_iter = 2000, rho = 0.99)
lag1_autocorrelation <- function(x) stats::cor(x[-1], x[-length(x)])
c(
  rho_0 = lag1_autocorrelation(draws_indep[, 1]),
  rho_0.99 = lag1_autocorrelation(draws_corr[, 1])
) |>
  round(3)
```

With $\corpar = 0$,
successive draws of $\param_1$ are nearly uncorrelated.
With $\corpar = 0.99$,
each full conditional has standard deviation $\sqrt{1 - 0.99^2} \approx 0.14$,
so each update moves only a short way along the narrow ridge
where the target puts its probability,
and successive draws are almost perfectly correlated:
2,000 such draws carry far less information about the target
than 2,000 independent ones.
:::
